TUTOR: Good morning, Lucy, Omar. You're working on the assignment about school meals. How's it going?
LUCY: We've decided to compare school lunches in two countries: Japan and the UK.
TUTOR: Why those two?
OMAR: Japan is often held up as a model because lunches are cooked fresh and children help serve them. And we both went to school in the UK, so we know that system.
TUTOR: Fine, but don't rely on your own memories. Things have changed a lot in British schools over the last decade.
LUCY: We know. We're using government reports on nutritional standards.
TUTOR: Good. And for Japan?
OMAR: That's harder. A lot of the detailed material is only in Japanese. I've found some English summaries, but they're quite general.
TUTOR: Is there anyone in the department who reads Japanese?
LUCY: Actually, a classmate, Haruka, offered to help us with a couple of key documents.
TUTOR: Excellent — but acknowledge her help in the report. Now, what's your main argument?
OMAR: We think the biggest difference isn't the food itself, but the way lunch is treated as part of education — children learn about where food comes from.
LUCY: I'm not totally convinced. I think cost matters more. Japanese schools may simply spend more per meal.
TUTOR: That's a factual question you can check. If the spending turns out to be similar, Omar's argument becomes stronger. If not, you'll need to discuss both.
OMAR: That's fair.
TUTOR: Also think about whether the Japanese model could actually work in the UK. What would the barriers be?
LUCY: Kitchens, for one. Lots of British schools no longer have full kitchens; meals are delivered from central units.
OMAR: And timetables. Japanese pupils often have a longer lunch break, which allows for serving and cleaning up.
TUTOR: Both excellent points. Make that the final section of your report. Oh, and keep any tables of nutritional data short; put the full figures in an appendix.
LUCY: Will do.
question: Why does the tutor warn against using personal memories?
choices: Memories are not accepted as evidence.
British school meals have changed recently.
The students went to different schools.
answer: British school meals have changed recently.
explanation: Things have changed a lot in British schools over the last decade と 言っている。

TUTOR: So, Rosa and Ben, your seminar presentation is on child labour during industrialisation in Britain. What angle are you taking?
ROSA: We wanted to look at why the 1833 Factory Act was passed. Most textbooks credit the campaigners, but we think economic factors mattered too.
TUTOR: Interesting. What kind of economic factors?
BEN: New machinery meant some factory owners needed fewer child workers anyway. So limiting child labour cost them less than it would have done earlier.
TUTOR: That's a debated position. You'll need to support it with evidence, not just logic.
ROSA: We've found employment records from two textile mills in Lancashire. They show the number of children falling before the Act.
TUTOR: Two mills is a small sample. Be careful about generalising to the whole country.
BEN: We'll present it as a case study rather than a national picture.
TUTOR: Good. What about the campaigners? You can't ignore them.
ROSA: No, we'll acknowledge them. Our argument is that their success depended partly on timing — they pushed at a moment when resistance was weaker.
TUTOR: That's a more nuanced claim and easier to defend. What primary sources are you using?
BEN: Parliamentary reports, mainly. They include interviews with children, which are very powerful.
TUTOR: They are, but remember who conducted those interviews and why. Some inspectors had strong opinions, and the questions could be quite leading.
ROSA: So we should treat them critically, rather than as neutral evidence.
TUTOR: Exactly. How will you divide the presentation?
BEN: Rosa will do the context and the campaigners, and I'll do the mill records.
ROSA: And we'll both answer questions, obviously.
TUTOR: I'd suggest ending with a question for the group, to start the discussion. That's what a seminar is for.
BEN: Something like, "Do laws change society, or does society change first and the laws follow?"
TUTOR: Perfect. That'll get people talking. And remember to keep to twenty minutes; the next group needs time too.
question: What do the students want to argue about the 1833 Act?
choices: Economic changes also contributed to it.
It was ignored by most factory owners.
answer: Economic changes also contributed to it.
explanation: we think economic factors mattered too と Rosa。運動家の 役割は 否定せず 認める。
tags: IELTS Listening Part3 history seminar industrialisation presentation

TUTOR: Let's review your design project. The brief was a solar-powered water pump for small farms. Where are you?
ZARA: We've got two possible designs. Design A uses a small panel and a battery, so it can pump at night. Design B has no battery; it just pumps when the sun is shining, into a raised storage tank.
TUTOR: And which are you leaning towards?
MARCUS: I preferred A at first, because it's more flexible. But Zara convinced me B is better.
ZARA: The battery is the most expensive part, and it needs replacing every few years. For farmers on low incomes, that's a real problem.
TUTOR: Good thinking. The tank stores energy as water instead. What about efficiency?
MARCUS: B loses a bit, because water can evaporate from the tank in hot weather. But we can add a simple cover to minimise that.
TUTOR: Have you thought about maintenance?
ZARA: Yes. We want to use standard parts that are available locally, so farmers don't depend on imports.
TUTOR: That's important. How are you testing the design?
MARCUS: We've built a small-scale prototype. We've run it outside for three days, but the weather's been cloudy, so the results are lower than real conditions.
TUTOR: Then use a lamp in the lab to simulate stronger sunlight, and compare. Just be clear in the report that it's a simulation.
ZARA: Good idea. Another issue is the height of the tank. Higher means more pressure for watering, but the pump uses more energy to lift the water.
TUTOR: That's your main trade-off. I'd like a graph showing flow rate against tank height. That should help you identify the optimal height.
MARCUS: OK. And the final report — should we include the battery design at all?
TUTOR: Yes. Explain why you rejected it. Examiners like to see that alternatives were considered.
ZARA: And the cost analysis?
TUTOR: Keep it simple: a table of parts and prices. Don't spend too long on it; it's only ten per cent of the mark.
question: Why did the students choose Design B?
choices: It can pump water at night.
It is more efficient in hot weather.
It avoids an expensive part that needs replacing.
answer: It avoids an expensive part that needs replacing.
explanation: battery が 高く 数年ごとに 交換が 必要と Zara が 説明し、B に 決めた。夜の くみ上げは A の 利点。
tags: IELTS Listening Part3 engineering design solar water-pump

TUTOR: So, Leila and Sam, you're researching how news apps choose which stories to show people. How's the literature review going?
LEILA: Well, there's a lot written about "filter bubbles" — the idea that algorithms only show people views they already agree with.
SAM: But the empirical evidence is actually quite mixed. Several large studies found that most people still see a fairly wide range of sources.
TUTOR: So the popular idea may be exaggerated. That's a good tension to build your review around. What's your own study going to do?
LEILA: We want to set up new accounts on two news apps and "train" them by only clicking on one type of story — say, sport — and then see how the front page changes.
TUTOR: Interesting. How many accounts?
SAM: We were thinking four on each app: two trained on sport, two on politics.
TUTOR: You'll also need some accounts you don't train at all, as a comparison.
LEILA: A control group. Of course. We'll add two untrained accounts per app.
TUTOR: Good. How long will you run it?
SAM: Two weeks. Is that enough?
TUTOR: It's probably the minimum. And bear in mind that news varies from day to day. If there's a major event, every account will show it.
LEILA: So we should compare accounts on the same day, rather than comparing different days.
TUTOR: Exactly. Now, the apps' terms of service. Have you checked that creating test accounts is allowed?
SAM: Not yet. I'll check this week.
TUTOR: Please do, before you start. And ethics — since there are no human participants, it should be straightforward, but you still need to submit a form.
LEILA: We'll do it. One more thing — how should we classify stories? Some are hard to label.
TUTOR: Write clear definitions for each category before you begin, and both of you label a sample independently. If you disagree often, refine the definitions.
SAM: That makes sense. It'll improve the reliability.

choices: The evidence for them is inconsistent.
There has been very little research.
answer: The evidence for them is inconsistent.
explanation: the empirical evidence is actually quite mixed と Sam が 言っている。

TUTOR: OK, the coastal fieldtrip is next month. Tara, Felix, Ming — you're the group studying erosion at Hollow Bay. Have you planned your methods?
TARA: We're going to measure how far the cliff top has moved back by comparing it with old maps and aerial photographs.
TUTOR: Good. Where will you get those?
FELIX: The county archive has maps going back to 1900. And there's a free online collection of aerial photos from the 1940s onwards.
TUTOR: Be careful with the early maps. They weren't always accurate, so treat small differences with caution.
MING: We'll focus on the bigger changes, then. We also wanted to measure the beach profile — the slope of the beach at different points.
TUTOR: Why?
MING: Because a wider, higher beach protects the cliff by absorbing wave energy. Where the beach is narrow, we'd expect faster erosion.
TUTOR: Excellent hypothesis. What equipment?
TARA: Ranging poles and a tape measure. We'll take readings every two metres from the cliff base to the sea.
TUTOR: Make sure you go at low tide, otherwise you won't reach the lower beach. Check the tide tables before you set a time.
FELIX: We will. We were also thinking of interviewing local residents about the sea wall the council is proposing.
TUTOR: That could be interesting, but it's a different kind of project — more human geography. Will you have time?
TARA: Probably not. Maybe we should save that for the dissertation.
TUTOR: I think that's wise. Focus on the physical data.
MING: What about safety? Some of the cliffs are unstable.
TUTOR: Stay at least ten metres from the base of the cliff, and don't climb on any fallen material. Helmets are compulsory, and you'll borrow them from the department.
FELIX: And who's writing the risk assessment?
TARA: I'll do it. I did one last term.
TUTOR: Send it to me by Friday, please, so I can sign it off. Without my signature, the group can't go on the trip.

TUTOR: Hello, Noor and Alex. You're investigating how remote working affects people's sense of belonging at work. Where are you up to?
NOOR: We've finished our interviews. Twelve people, all office workers who've worked mainly from home for at least a year.
TUTOR: How did you recruit them?
ALEX: Through social media, mostly. Which is a limitation, we know — they're probably more comfortable with technology than average.
TUTOR: Good that you've recognised that. What are the main themes so far?
NOOR: The strongest one is about informal contact. Almost everyone said they miss the small conversations — in the kitchen, in the corridor — more than formal meetings.
ALEX: And several said that online meetings feel more efficient, but less human. They get the work done, but nobody chats.
TUTOR: Was there anything unexpected?
NOOR: Yes. We assumed younger workers would adapt more easily, but in our sample it was the opposite. Older people who already had strong relationships at work felt more connected.
TUTOR: That's interesting. Why do you think that might be?
ALEX: Probably because the younger ones never had the chance to build those relationships in person in the first place.
TUTOR: Plausible. Be cautious about how strongly you state it, though, with only twelve participants.
NOOR: We'll describe it as a pattern worth further research.
TUTOR: How are you analysing the transcripts?
ALEX: Thematic analysis. We each coded four transcripts independently first, then met to agree a coding framework, and applied it to the rest.
TUTOR: That's a solid approach. Keep a record of any disagreements and how you resolved them; it strengthens your methodology section.
NOOR: We've been doing that in a shared document.
TUTOR: And quotations — use them, but choose ones that genuinely represent a theme, not just the most dramatic.
ALEX: Good point. Some of the most quotable things were said by just one person.
TUTOR: Then make that clear. Right, I'd like a full draft in a fortnight.

choices: Too few people agreed to take part.
Participants may be unusually confident with technology.
All participants worked for one company.
answer: Participants may be unusually confident with technology.
explanation: through social media → more comfortable with technology than average と Alex が 言っている。
